4.1: That which rules within, when it is in accordance with nature, is so disposed towards the events that happen that it always easily adapts itself to what is possible and presented to it. For it needs no fixed material, but it moves towards its purpose, under certain conditions, however; and it makes material for itself out of whatever opposes it, as fire takes hold of what falls into it, by which a small light would have been put out; but when the fire is strong, it soon makes its own the matter heaped on it, and consumes it, and rises higher by means of this very material.
4.2: Let no act be done without a purpose, nor other than according to the perfect principles of art.
4.3:
Men seek retreats for themselves, houses in the country, the seashore, and the mountains; and you too tend to long for such things very much. But this is entirely the mark of the most ordinary sort of men, for it is in your power, whenever you choose, to retire into yourself. For nowhere does a man retire with more quiet or more freedom from trouble than into his own soul, especially when he has within him thoughts such that by looking into them he is immediately in perfect tranquillity; and I say that tranquillity is nothing other than the good ordering of the mind. Constantly, then, give yourself this retreat, and renew yourself; and let your principles be brief and fundamental, so that, as soon as you return to them, they will be enough to cleanse the soul completely, and to send you back free from all discontent with the things you return to. For what are you discontented with? With the badness of men? Bring to mind this conclusion: that rational beings exist for one another, that to endure is a part of justice, and that men do wrong involuntarily; and consider how many already, after mutual hostility, suspicion, hatred, and fighting, have been laid out dead and reduced to ashes; and be quiet at last.—But perhaps you are dissatisfied with what is assigned to you out of the universe.—Recall this alternative: either there is providence, or there are atoms, a chance coming-together of things; or remember the arguments by which it has been proved that the world is a kind of political community; and be quiet at last.—But perhaps bodily things will still take hold of you.—Consider then further that the mind does not mingle with the breath, whether it moves gently or violently, once it has drawn itself apart and discovered its own power; and think also of all that you have heard and agreed to about pain and pleasure; and be quiet at last.—But perhaps the desire for the thing called fame will torment you.—See how soon everything is forgotten, and look at the chaos of infinite time on either side of the present, and the emptiness of applause, and the fickleness and lack of judgement in those who claim to give praise, and the narrowness of the space within which it is confined; and be quiet at last. For the whole earth is a point, and how small a corner of it is this place where you live, and how few are there in it, and what kind of people are they who will praise you?

This, then, remains: remember to retire into this little territory of your own, and above all do not distract or strain yourself, but be free, and look at things as a man, as a human being, as a citizen, as a mortal. And among the things most ready to hand, to which you will turn, let there be these two. One is that things do not touch the soul, for they are external and remain unmoved; our disturbances come only from the opinion within. The other is that all these things you see change immediately and will no longer be; and constantly bear in mind how many of these changes you have already witnessed. The universe is change: life is opinion.
4.4: If our intellectual part is common to us all, then reason too, in respect of which we are rational beings, is common: if this is so, common too is the reason which commands us what to do and what not to do; if this is so, there is a common law too; if this is so, we are fellow citizens; if this is so, we are members of some political community; if this is so, the world is in a way a state. For of what other common political community will anyone say that the whole human race are members? And from there, from this common political community, come our very intellectual faculty and reasoning faculty and our capacity for law; or where else do they come from? For as my earthly part is a portion given to me from a certain earth, and what is watery from another element, and what is hot and fiery from some particular source (for nothing comes out of nothing, just as nothing returns to non-existence), so too the intellectual part comes from some source.
4.5: Death, like birth, is a mystery of nature: a putting together out of the same elements, and a taking apart into the same; and in no way a thing any man should be ashamed of, for it is not contrary to the nature of a reasonable being, nor contrary to the reason of our constitution.
4.6: It is natural that these things should be done by such people; it is a matter of necessity; and if a man will not have it so, he will not allow the fig tree to have juice. But by all means bear this in mind, that within a very short time both you and he will be dead; and soon not even your names will be left behind.
4.7: Take away your opinion, and then the complaint “I have been harmed” is taken away. Take away the complaint “I have been harmed,” and the harm is taken away.
4.8: That which does not make a man worse than he was does not make his life worse either, nor does it harm him, either from without or from within.
4.9: The nature of what is universally useful has been compelled to do this.
4.10: Consider that everything that happens, happens justly, and if you observe carefully, you will find it to be so. I do not mean only with respect to the continuity of the series of things, but with respect to what is just, and as if it were done by one who gives each thing its due value. Observe, then, as you have begun; and whatever you do, do it together with this: being good, in the sense in which a man is properly understood to be good. Keep to this in every action.
4.11: Do not hold the opinion of things that the man who wrongs you holds, or the one he wishes you to hold, but look at them as they truly are.
4.12: A man should always have these two rules ready: the first, to do only whatever the reason of the ruling and law-giving faculty may suggest for the good of men; the second, to change your opinion if there is anyone at hand who sets you right and moves you from any opinion. But this change of opinion must come only from a real conviction, as of what is just or of common benefit, and the like, not because it seems pleasant or brings reputation.
4.13: Do you have reason? I have.—Why then do you not use it? For if this does its own work, what else do you want?
4.14: You have existed as a part. You will disappear into that which produced you; or rather, you will be taken back into its seed-giving principle by transformation.
4.15: Many grains of frankincense on the same altar: one falls first, another falls later; but it makes no difference.
4.16: Within ten days you will seem a god to those to whom you are now a beast and an ape, if you return to your principles and the worship of reason.
4.17: Do not act as if you were going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over you. While you live, while it is in your power, be good.
4.18: How much trouble he avoids who does not look to see what his neighbour says or does or thinks, but only at what he does himself, that it may be just and pure; or, as Agathon says, do not look round at the corrupt morals of others, but run straight along the line without swerving from it.
4.19: He who has a burning desire for fame after death does not consider that every one of those who remember him will himself also die very soon; and then again those who have succeeded them, until the whole memory has been put out as it passes through men who foolishly admire and then perish. But suppose that those who will remember are even immortal, and that the memory will be immortal, what then is this to you? And I do not mean what is it to the dead, but what is it to the living? What is praise, except indeed in so far as it has a certain usefulness? For you now reject, at the wrong time, the gift of nature, clinging to something else....
4.20: Everything which is in any way beautiful is beautiful in itself, and complete in itself, not having praise as part of itself. A thing is made neither worse nor better by being praised. I say this also of the things which ordinary people call beautiful, for example, material things and works of art. That which is truly beautiful needs nothing; no more than law, no more than truth, no more than kindness or modesty. Which of these things is beautiful because it is praised, or spoiled by being blamed? Is something like an emerald made worse than it was if it is not praised? Or gold, ivory, purple, a lyre, a little knife, a flower, a shrub?
4.21:
If souls continue to exist, how does the air hold them from all eternity?—But how does the earth hold the bodies of those who have been buried since times so remote? For as here the change of these bodies after a certain length of time, whatever it may be, and their dissolution make room for other dead bodies, so the souls which are moved into the air, after lasting for some time, are transformed and dispersed, and take on a fiery nature by being received into the seed-giving intelligence of the universe, and in this way make room for the fresh souls which come to live there. And this is the answer a man might give on the assumption that souls continue to exist. But we must think not only of the number of bodies which are buried in this way, but also of the number of animals which are eaten daily by us and by the other animals. For what a number are consumed, and so in a way buried in the bodies of those who feed on them! And yet this earth receives them, because of the changes of these bodies into blood, and their transformations into the airy or the fiery element.

What is the way to investigate the truth in this matter? By dividing things into what is material and what is the cause of form, the formal.
4.22: Do not be whirled about, but in every movement have regard to justice, and whenever an impression comes, keep hold of your power of understanding.
4.23: Everything is in harmony with me which is in harmony with you, O Universe. Nothing is too early or too late for me which is in due time for you. Everything is fruit to me which your seasons bring, O Nature: from you are all things, in you are all things, to you all things return. The poet says, Dear city of Cecrops; and will you not say, Dear city of Zeus?
4.24: Busy yourself with few things, says the philosopher, if you would be tranquil.—But consider whether it would not be better to say: Do what is necessary, and whatever the reason of a naturally social being requires, and as it requires. For this brings not only the tranquillity which comes from doing well, but also that which comes from doing few things. For since most of what we say and do is unnecessary, if a man takes this away, he will have more leisure and less unease. So on every occasion a man should ask himself: Is this one of the unnecessary things? Now a man should take away not only unnecessary acts, but also unnecessary thoughts, for then superfluous acts will not follow.
4.25: Try how the life of the good man suits you, the life of one who is satisfied with his share of the whole, and satisfied with his own just acts and kindly disposition.
4.26: Have you seen those things? Look at these too. Do not disturb yourself. Make yourself all simplicity. Does anyone do wrong? It is to himself that he does the wrong. Has anything happened to you? Well; out of the universe, from the beginning, everything that happens has been allotted and spun out for you. In a word, your life is short. You must make the most of the present with the help of reason and justice. Be sober in your relaxation.
4.27: Either it is a well-ordered universe or a chaos heaped together, but still a universe. But can a kind of order exist in you, and disorder in the All? And this too when all things are so separated and dispersed and in sympathy.
4.28: A black character, an effeminate character, a stubborn character, beastly, childish, brutish, stupid, false, coarse, fraudulent, tyrannical.
4.29: If he is a stranger to the universe who does not know what is in it, he is no less a stranger who does not know what is going on in it. He is a runaway who flees from social reason; he is blind who shuts the eyes of understanding; he is poor who needs another, and does not have from himself all the things that are useful for life. He is an abscess on the universe who withdraws and separates himself from the reason of our common nature through being displeased with the things that happen, for the same nature produces this, and has produced you too: he is a piece torn off from the state who tears his own soul away from that of rational beings, which is one.
4.30: One is a philosopher without a tunic, and another without a book: here is another, half naked: I have no bread, he says, and I hold fast to reason—and I do not get a living out of my learning, and I hold fast to my reason.
4.31: Love the art, poor as it may be, which you have learned, and be content with it; and pass through the rest of life like one who has entrusted to the gods, with his whole soul, all that he has, making yourself neither the tyrant nor the slave of any man.
4.32: Consider, for example, the times of Vespasian. You will see all these things: people marrying, bringing up children, being sick, dying, making war, feasting, trading, farming the land, flattering, being stubbornly arrogant, suspecting, plotting, wishing for some to die, grumbling about the present, loving, piling up treasure, longing for the consulship, for kingly power. Well, then, that life of these people no longer exists at all. Again, move on to the times of Trajan. Again, all is the same. Their life too is gone. In the same way look also at the other ages of time and of whole nations, and see how many, after great efforts, soon fell and were dissolved into the elements. But most of all you should think of those you have known yourself, distracting themselves about idle things, neglecting to do what was in keeping with their proper constitution, and to hold firmly to this and be content with it. And here it is necessary to remember that the attention given to everything has its proper value and proportion. For then you will not be dissatisfied, if you apply yourself to smaller matters no further than is fitting.
4.33: The words which were once familiar are now outdated: so too the names of those who were famous long ago are now in a way outdated, Camillus, Caeso, Volesus, Leonnatus, and a little later Scipio and Cato too, then Augustus, then also Hadrianus and Antoninus. For all things soon pass away and become a mere tale, and complete oblivion soon buries them. And I say this of those who have shone in a wonderful way. As for the rest, as soon as they have breathed their last they are gone, and no one speaks of them. And, to conclude the matter, what is even an eternal remembrance? A mere nothing. What then is it that we ought to give our serious effort to? This one thing: just thoughts, and social acts, and words which never lie, and a disposition which gladly accepts all that happens, as necessary, as usual, as flowing from a principle and source of the same kind.
4.34: Willingly give yourself up to Clotho, one of the Fates, allowing her to spin your thread into whatever things she pleases.
4.35: Everything lasts only for a day, both that which remembers and that which is remembered.
4.36: Observe constantly that all things come about by change, and get used to considering that the nature of the universe loves nothing so much as to change the things which are and to make new things like them. For everything that exists is in a way the seed of what will be. But you are thinking only of seeds which are cast into the earth or into a womb: but this is a very crude notion.
4.37: You will soon die, and you are not yet simple, nor free from disturbance, nor free from suspicion of being hurt by external things, nor kindly disposed towards all; nor do you yet place wisdom only in acting justly.
4.38: Examine men's ruling principles, even those of the wise: what kind of things they avoid, and what kind they pursue.
4.39: What is evil to you does not exist in the ruling principle of another; nor yet in any turn and change of your bodily covering. Where is it, then? It is in that part of you in which lies the power of forming opinions about evils. Let this power, then, not form such opinions, and all is well. And even if what is nearest to it, the poor body, is cut, burnt, filled with pus and rot, still let the part which forms opinions about these things be quiet; that is, let it judge that nothing is either bad or good which can happen equally to the bad man and the good. For that which happens equally to him who lives contrary to nature and to him who lives according to nature is neither according to nature nor contrary to nature.
4.40: Constantly regard the universe as one living being, having one substance and one soul; and observe how all things relate to one perception, the perception of this one living being; and how all things act with one movement; and how all things are the cooperating causes of all things which exist; observe too the continuous spinning of the thread and the weaving of the web.
4.41: You are a little soul carrying around a corpse, as Epictetus used to say.
4.42: It is no evil for things to undergo change, and no good for things to exist as a result of change.
4.43: Time is like a river made up of the events which happen, and a violent stream; for as soon as a thing has been seen, it is carried away, and another comes in its place, and this will be carried away too.
4.44: Everything that happens is as familiar and well known as the rose in spring and the fruit in summer; for such is disease, and death, and slander, and treachery, and whatever else delights fools or annoys them.
4.45: In the series of things, those which follow are always well fitted to those which have gone before: for this series is not like a mere list of unconnected things, which has only a necessary sequence, but it is a rational connection: and as all existing things are arranged together harmoniously, so the things which come into existence show no mere succession, but a certain wonderful relationship.
4.46: Always remember the saying of Heraclitus, that the death of earth is to become water, and the death of water is to become air, and the death of air is to become fire, and the reverse. And think too of the man who forgets where the way leads, and that men quarrel with that with which they are most constantly in contact, the reason which governs the universe; and the things they meet with every day seem strange to them: and consider that we ought not to act and speak as if we were asleep, for even in sleep we seem to act and speak; and that we ought not, like children who learn from their parents, simply to act and speak as we have been taught.
4.47: If any god told you that you will die tomorrow, or certainly the day after tomorrow, you would not care much whether it was on the third day or tomorrow, unless you were extremely mean-spirited; for how small the difference is! So think it no great thing to die after as many years as you can name rather than tomorrow.
4.48: Think continually how many doctors are dead after often frowning over the sick; and how many astrologers after predicting the deaths of others with great pretensions; and how many philosophers after endless discourses on death or immortality; how many heroes after killing thousands; and how many tyrants who have used their power over men's lives with terrible arrogance, as if they were immortal; and how many cities are entirely dead, so to speak, Helice and Pompeii and Herculaneum, and countless others. Add to the count all whom you have known, one after another. One man, after burying another, has been laid out dead, and another buries him; and all this in a short time. In short, always observe how short-lived and worthless human things are, and what was yesterday a little mucus will tomorrow be a mummy or ashes. Pass, then, through this little space of time in keeping with nature, and end your journey content, as an olive falls when it is ripe, blessing nature who produced it, and thanking the tree on which it grew.
4.49:
Be like the headland against which the waves continually break, but it stands firm and tames the fury of the water around it.

Am I unhappy because this has happened to me? Not so, but I am happy, though this has happened to me, because I remain free from pain, neither crushed by the present nor fearing the future. For such a thing as this might have happened to any man; but not every man would have remained free from pain on such an occasion. Why then is that a misfortune rather than this a good fortune? And do you in all cases call something a man's misfortune which is not a departure from man's nature? And does a thing seem to you to be a departure from man's nature when it is not contrary to the will of man's nature? Well, you know the will of nature. Will this, then, which has happened prevent you from being just, generous, self-controlled, prudent, secure against thoughtless opinions and falsehood; will it prevent you from having modesty, freedom, and everything else by whose presence man's nature gains all that is its own? Remember too, on every occasion which leads you to irritation, to apply this principle: not that this is a misfortune, but that to bear it nobly is good fortune.
4.50: It is a common, but still a useful, help towards contempt of death to call to mind those who have clung stubbornly to life. What more, then, have they gained than those who died early? Certainly they lie in their tombs somewhere at last, Cadicianus, Fabius, Julianus, Lepidus, or anyone else like them, who carried many out to be buried, and then were carried out themselves. Altogether the interval between birth and death is small; and consider with how much trouble, and in the company of what sort of people, and in how feeble a body, this interval is laboriously passed. Do not, then, consider life a thing of any value. For look at the immensity of time behind you, and at the time which is before you, another boundless space. In this infinity, then, what is the difference between one who lives three days and one who lives three generations?
4.51: Always run by the short way; and the short way is the natural one: so say and do everything in keeping with the soundest reason. For such a purpose frees a man from trouble, and conflict, and all scheming and showy display.
